It describes alarm systems, evacuation routes and assembly points, headcount procedures, rescue and medical response, and staff training requirements. The plan must comply with OSHA 1910.38 and Oregon OSHA rules.

        · Missing contact name or title for plan information and duties
            OSHA 1910.38(c)(6) requires the plan to include the name or job title of every employee who may be contacted by employees who need more information about the plan or an explanation of their duties. This document does not list such names or titles.
            what it needs: Add a section identifying specific employees (by name or title) who can answer questions about the plan and employee duties—for example, the facilities lead or a safety officer.
            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.38(c)(6)
        · Missing procedures for employees remaining to operate critical plant operations
            OSHA 1910.38(c)(3) requires the plan to include procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations before they evacuate. This plan does not describe such procedures.

            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.165(b)

      what the reading said it is: This is a daily inspection log for a propane-powered Toyota forklift (FL-2) operated at the Portland warehouse. The log documents pre-shift safety inspections per OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) covering tires, forks, mast, horn, lights, seat belt, brakes, steering, propane tank, fire extinguisher, data plate, and overhead guard. The company is required to maintain this inspection record as evidence that defective equipment is identified and removed from service before use.
      WHAT THE READING FOUND WRONG WITH IT (3) — these are already findings; carry them, do not re-find them:
        · Missing inspections for September 3–6 and September 12–13
            The log shows entries for September 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires that powered industrial trucks be examined before being placed in service and shall be examined at least daily. The hour meter shows the truck was in operation on the missing days (hours rose from 4,819 on September 2 to 4,834 on September 7, and from 4,860 on September 11 to 4,873 on September 15), but no inspection records exist for September 3, 4, 5, 6, 12, or 13. This is a gap in documentation required by OSHA.
            what it needs: Inspect and log the truck before each shift, every day, including weekends and holidays. If the truck was operated on September 3–6 and 12–13 but no shift occurred, document that explicitly (e.g., 'Not in service' or 'Weekend – no operations'). Going forward, do not operate the truck without first recording a pre-shift inspection.
            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7)
        · Horn defect not removed from service
            On September 9, the inspection log shows an 'X' in the Horn column with the operator note 'Horn not working.' However, the truck continued to be used the next day (September 10, inspected by J.R. with all items marked OK, including horn). OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) requires that trucks showing a defective condition adversely affecting safety shall not be placed in service, and defects shall be immediately reported and corrected. A non-functioning horn is a safety defect that should have removed the truck from service until repaired.
            what it needs: When a defect is found during pre-shift inspection, do not place the truck in service. Mark it out of service, notify supervision immediately, document the defect and the date removed from service, repair it, and re-inspect before returning it to use. The September 10 entry should show that either (a) the horn was repaired overnight and re-tested on September 10, or (b) the truck remained out of service.
            the rule: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7)
        · Supervisor review signature missing  [worked out from the document, not stated in it]
            The log template includes a line for 'Supervisor review: ______________________ Date: __________', but no supervisor has signed or dated this section. OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) does not explicitly require supervisor sign-off, but best practice and many state inspection protocols expect documented supervisory review of inspection records to ensure accountability and that defects are acted upon. The absence of a signature leaves no evidence that a supervisor has reviewed the log or verified that noted defects were corrected.
            what it needs: Have the appropriate supervisor review the monthly inspection log and sign it with the date. Document the supervisor's name and title. This provides evidence of management oversight and ensures that any defects noted (like the September 9 horn failure) were tracked and corrected before the truck returned to service.
            the rule: Oregon OSHA guidance; 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) best practices
      WHAT THIS DOCUMENT OBLIGES THEM TO KEEP DOING (3), read out of the document itself:
        · 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — Daily pre-shift inspection of Toyota 8FGU25 (FL-2) before placing in service
            the evidence you would expect to see: Pre-shift inspection log with date, time/shift, checklist items (tires, forks, mast, horn, lights, belt, brakes, steering, LPG tank, fire extinguisher, data plate, guard), operator initials, and any defects noted. Log must show inspection before the truck is used each day.
        · 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — Removal of defective equipment from service
            the evidence you would expect to see: When an 'X' or defect is marked on the inspection log, the truck must not be placed in service for the next shift. Evidence would be: (a) documentation that the defect was corrected before the next inspection (repair ticket, maintenance record), (b) re-inspection showing the item as OK, or (c) the truck marked 'Out of Service' or 'Not Inspected' until repaired.
        · 29 CFR 1910.178(l) — Operator certification and training
            the evidence you would expect to see: Training and evaluation records for each operator; the log shows M.C. (M. Chen, certified 2024-03-11, evaluation due 2027-03-11) and J.R. (J. Rivera, certified 2025-06-02, evaluation due 2028-06-02). Evidence: initial training records, evaluation completion dates, proof of re-evaluation at least every 3 years.

        · J. Rivera (J.R.) forklift operator re-evaluation due — 2028-06-02 (recurring)
        · M. Chen (M.C.) forklift operator re-evaluation due — 2027-03-11 (recurring)
      WHAT THE READING SAID A COMPANY LIKE THIS USUALLY ALSO HOLDS (3) —
        a suggestion from similar companies, NOT a checked requirement:
        · Forklift certification or in-service equipment record — A document showing the truck's original certification date, manufacturer certification, any modifications, and current permit/registration status
        · Maintenance and repair log for forklift FL-2 — The September 9 horn defect should be paired with a maintenance work order or repair ticket showing when the horn was fixed, by whom, and the date returned to service
